items.title: Battle turns
items.summary: The fixed half-second timing units used to register and resolve battle actions.

content.heading: The smallest timing unit
body: The current Trainer Battle system measures timing in turns. One turn lasts 0.5 seconds, and Fast Attack durations are expressed as whole turns.
Actions resolve from the shared battle state and turn order. Normal variation in network or device timing does not change the result for identical decisions in an identical state.

content.heading: Read the timeline
body: Each numbered cell is one turn. The same six turns equal three seconds of battle time.

content.heading: Key point
body: Turn numbers describe ordering. Seconds describe elapsed time. Keep the two separate when reconstructing an incident; a visual delay is not a different battle rule.

items.title: Fast Attack duration
items.summary: How a Fast Attack's duration controls action availability, alignment, and its impact turn.

content.heading: Duration locks the user
body: A Fast Attack starts on its registration turn and occupies the user for its listed duration. Its damage and energy are not applied merely because the move started; they wait for the appropriate end-of-turn impact.
A 2-turn attack and a 3-turn attack therefore reach their next action windows and impact points at different times.

content.heading: Two-turn versus three-turn alignment
body: The rows begin together. They realign after six turns, when three 2-turn moves and two 3-turn moves have completed.

content.heading: Why it matters
body: Duration determines both the next legal action window and where Fast Attack impact appears on the reconstructed timeline. The action can be pending before that impact.

items.title: Fast Attack impact
items.summary: When Fast Attack damage and energy are applied under the current end-of-turn rule.

content.heading: Impact turn
body: Fast Attack damage is applied at the end of the appropriate turn after the move's duration. Energy is granted at the same moment as that damage. A Fast Attack that has started but not reached this point is a pending Fast.
Pending status is a scheduled resolution, not an immediate knockout. The target can still have a legal Charged or switch action before impact when the current turn sequence permits it.
Fast Attack events that impact on the same turn are evaluated from the state at that impact phase, so simultaneous damage can produce a simultaneous knockout.

content.heading: Three-turn Fast Attack
body: A move registered on turn 1 with duration 3 reaches its impact on turn 3.

content.heading: Key point
body: Registration, pending status, impact, and the next ready turn are separate facts. Use the event marker and state snapshot together when reviewing timing.

items.title: Energy generation and spending
items.summary: How Fast Attack energy is gained, capped, and spent on Charged Attacks.

content.heading: Gain at Fast Attack impact
body: Fast Attack energy is added when that Fast Attack's damage is applied at impact. Stored energy is capped at 100; any gain beyond the cap is not retained.

A Charged Attack becomes available when the Pokémon has enough energy and reaches its legal action window. The Charged action starts at the beginning of the next turn, and resolving it spends the listed cost.
Energy remains with that Pokémon until it is spent on a Charged Attack or the Pokémon faints. Energy cannot be transferred to another Pokémon, and switching out does not remove stored energy.

content.heading: Example
body: A Pokémon at 96 energy uses a Fast Attack that grants 8 energy. The resulting total is 100, not 104. A 45-energy Charged Attack would then leave 55 energy.

content.heading: Key point
body: Having enough energy is necessary but not sufficient: the Pokémon must also be at a legal action window.

items.title: Charged Attack Priority (CAP)
items.summary: How Charged Attack registration and simultaneous priority work under the current turn model.

content.heading: Compare priority Attack
body: A Charged Attack is registered in the decision window but starts at the beginning of the next turn. Its damage and effects resolve before the end of Fast Attacks completing during that Charged sequence.

When both sides register a Charged Attack in the same decision window, Charged Attack Priority compares each side's priority Attack value; the higher value starts first. Temporary Attack stage changes during battle do not change CAP order in the simulator, and displayed CP does not decide it. Defense changes do not affect CAP; they only affect damage.
A pending Fast does not turn the old DRE discussion into a random exception: the current turn sequence deterministically decides which legal Charged action resolves before the Fast impact.

content.heading: Resolution order
body: Both Charged Attacks are registered in the same decision window.
Priority Attack is compared and the higher-Attack side starts first on the next turn.
The battle state is checked before the second registered action continues, and pending Fast impacts remain ordered by the same deterministic turn sequence.

content.heading: Equal priority Attack
body: Equal priority Attack is retained as a tied-CAP condition in review metadata. Treat the tie itself as relevant evidence rather than inferring an advantage from species name or CP.

items.title: Attack and Defense stages
items.summary: The bounded battle modifiers applied to Attack and Defense.

content.heading: Stage range
body: Attack and Defense stages are tracked independently from −4 through +4. Effects cannot raise or lower a stat beyond those limits.
Positive Attack stages increase outgoing damage calculations. Positive Defense stages increase the defending value; negative stages act in the opposite direction.

content.heading: Multiplier pattern
body: The simulator uses (4 + stage) / 4 for non-negative stages and 4 / (4 − stage) for negative stages. For example, +1 is 1.25× and −1 is 0.8×.

content.heading: CAP interaction
body: CAP compares priority Attack, not temporary Attack stages. Defense changes affect damage, not CAP itself.

items.title: Charged Attack timing
items.summary: How registration, next-turn start, and Fast completion fit together.

content.heading: Register now, start next turn
body: A Charged Attack is selected and registered in the current decision window, then begins at the start of the next turn. It is not an instant action on the trigger turn.
During the Charged sequence, the Charged Attack's damage and effects apply before the end-of-turn impact of a Fast Attack completing in that sequence.

content.heading: Why the distinction matters
body: A Fast Attack may already be scheduled to deal lethal damage at the end of the turn. If the target has a legal Charged action in the current window, the next-turn Charged sequence can resolve according to the current timing rule before that pending impact; pending does not mean immediate KO.

content.heading: Deterministic priority
body: The result is determined by registration, action readiness, Charged Attack Priority, and the pending impact turn. It is not decided by which device or connection delivered an input a fraction earlier.

items.title: Pending Fast damage
items.summary: How a started Fast Attack is scheduled, displayed, and resolved.

content.heading: Registered is not resolved
body: A Fast Attack can be registered and in progress before its damage reaches the end-of-turn impact. That scheduled event is a pending Fast. A pending Fast can be lethal without being an immediate knockout.
The HP bar or timeline may briefly show pending damage before the game applies it. The damage animation is feedback after application, not a second damage event.

content.heading: What can happen before impact
body: Check whether the target has a legal Charged or switch action in the current window.
Resolve that action according to the next-turn, priority, and switch rules.
Apply the pending Fast at its scheduled impact using the current valid battle state.

content.heading: Impact uses the current target state
body: Pokémon A has a Fast Attack pending on Pokémon B. Pokémon B uses a Charged Attack that lowers its own Defense before the pending Fast impact resolves. When A's Fast lands, it hits B and uses B's current Defense stage at impact time.

content.heading: A denied impact is not a second knockout
body: If the Fast source is no longer valid or alive before impact under the applicable battle state, the registered event can be denied. Registered, resolved, and denied are different statuses; a denied event must not create a duplicate KO marker.

items.title: Switching and damage transfer
items.summary: How voluntary, forced, and damage-absorbing switches are ordered.

content.heading: The switch is applied before damage
body: Under the current rules, a legal switch is processed before the pending damage it is intended to absorb. When a Pokémon switches during the same turn an opponent Fast Attack completes, the incoming Pokémon receives that Fast damage.
The same deterministic ordering applies across network and device conditions; the damage is not randomly assigned to the outgoing Pokémon.

content.heading: Switching into a Charged Attack
body: If a switch is made during the same turn an opponent's Charged Attack starts, the incoming Pokémon is the Charged Attack's target. The relevant action window, not a visual animation delay, determines the recipient.

content.heading: Three switch costs
body: A quick or manual voluntary switch costs one turn.
A forced switch after a knockout costs zero turns.
A legal switch at the end of a Charged Attack sequence costs zero turns and uses the post-Charged window.

items.title: Post-Charged switch window
items.summary: The immediate zero-turn switch window at the end of a Charged Attack sequence.

content.heading: A distinct immediate window
body: At the end of a Charged Attack sequence, an eligible Pokémon can use the post-Charged switch window without paying the normal one-turn voluntary-switch cost. This is a zero-turn switch, not a general exemption from switch cooldowns.

content.heading: Do not combine the windows
body: A normal quick or manual switch still costs one turn. A forced switch still costs zero turns. Only the applicable post-Charged window grants the immediate zero-turn voluntary switch.

content.heading: Short example
body: After the Charged sequence finishes, a player uses the available post-Charged switch before the next normal action. The replacement enters immediately; later voluntary switches return to the normal one-turn cost when their cooldown allows.

items.title: Disconnects and battle-state progression
items.summary: How the current system continues a battle when a client stops responding.

content.heading: The battle continues
body: Both players must connect before the battle begins. After that, the battle state continues to progress even if a client stops responding or a player stops touching the screen.
KO results, energy gain, alignment, and the timing of registered actions follow the same turn-based state progression rather than waiting for a new input or a faster connection.

content.heading: What this does not mean
body: A disconnect does not turn a pending Fast into an immediate impact or change the normal turn order. Reconstruct the recorded state and current turn order first; use the tournament review process for disputes.
